After considering the arguments made on behalf of both parties,
this Board now makes its decision as follows:
OPINION
In Valley Fruit v. Department of Revenue, 92 Wn. App. 413, 963
P. 2d 886 ( 1998), rev. den., 137 Wn'. 2d ' 1017 ( 1999), the Court of
Appeals, overruling this Board, determined that apple packers are
manufacturers," and thus can qualify for the then -existing distressed
areas sales deferral with respect to the purchase of manufacturing
equipment. RCW Chapter 82. 60; 82. 62. The Taxpayers had built
controlled atmosphere storage facilities and purchased apple packing
equipment in 1994, 1995, and 1996; but they had not applied for the
sales tax deferral prior to their investments because they believed
the Department would have denied their applications on the merits.
The Taxpayers now seek to compel the Department to accept their
applications and process them in accordance with the Valley Fruit
decision. We conclude the Department acted correctly when it declined
to process the Taxpayers' applications, and dismiss the Taxpayers'
appeals.
FINAL DECISION - Page 3 Dockets Nos. 00- 005 to 00- 009

FACTS1
The Taxpayers are engaged inthe apple packing and controlled
atmosphere storage warehouse business in Yakima County, Washington.
Between 1994 and 1997, they made substantial investments in construct-
ing new controlled atmosphere warehouses and installing new apple
packing equipment.
The Taxpayers were aware at the time they made these investments
that Washington permitted manufacturers in Yakima County to defer
sales tax on investments in new manufacturing buildings, machinery,
and equipment, and permitted such manufacturers to credit an amount
against their business and occupation ( B&O) taxes with respect to each
new employment position created at their manufacturing facility. The
Taxpayers were aware that they had to submit applications to, and
receive approval from, the Department prior to making their invest-
ments or hiring new employees. The Taxpayers were also aware that the
Department did not consider apple packing and controlled atmosphere
storage to be " manufacturing" as that term is defined in the deferral
and tax credit statutes, and would therefore deny their applications
out of hand. Consequently, the Taxpayers did not apply for the sales
tax deferral or the B&O tax credit at the time they made their

Fruit: investments in apple packing equipment and controlled atmos-
phere storage warehouses do not qualify for the distressed area sales
tax deferral and B&O tax credits.
HB 2295 had one other feature which bears on the issues in this
appeal. It was made expressly retroactive. " This act is intended to
clarify that this is the intent of the legislature both retroactively
and prospectively." HB 2295 § 4. The bill took effect on June 7,
1999. HB 2295 § 5. The purpose of the retroactive provision was not
so much to emphasize the Legislature' s and the Department' s disagree-
ment with the Court of Appeals' interpretation as it was to guarantee
that the unpalatable consequences flowing from a logical retroactive
extension of the Valley Fruit decision would not occur. 2
2 After Valley Fruit, the Department was in a tight spot. On the one
hand, it arguably would have been required as a matter of principled
tax administration ( i. e., according to the language of the tax code)
to apply the Valley Fruit result to B&O and sales tax obligations of
all agricultural processors and farmers—including those not located in
distressed areas. See Determination No. 99- 351 at 4, Ex. A, CPC' s
Notice of Appeal. Further, it would have been required to apply the
result ( arguably) retroactively to all periods still open under the
four-year statute of limitations and ( certainly) prospectively from
the date of the Court of Appeals' decision. On the other hand, given
the importance of Washington' s agricultural industry and the State' s
historical policy of favorable treatment tax -wise as compared to most
other industries, enforcing the tax code remorselessly according to
the letter of the law would upset reasonable expectations -and cause
severe, and in many cases irreparable, harm to many people. Whatever
one may suppose about the Legislature' s intent in enacting HB 2295, it
is clear that one of the Department' s main purposes in sponsoring the
bill was to extricate itself from what it believed was a no- win
situation.

After the passage of HB 2295, the Department' s Appeals Division
conducted a hearing on the Taxpayers' refund claims. It issued Deter-
mination No. 99- 351 on December 30, 1999, holding: ( 1) the Taxpayers'
failure to file applications for sales tax deferrals and B&O tax
credits prior to undertaking their investments in their apple packing
and controlled atmosphere storage business was fatal to the claim for
refund; and ( 2) the Department did not have the authority to pass on
the Taxpayers' claim that the retroactive provisions of HB 2295
infringed on their constitutional rights.
The Taxpayers timely filed Notices of Appeal with this Board.
ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS
I
Beginning in 1985, Washington permitted manufacturers in loca-
tions suffering high unemployment (" distressed areas") to defer
payment of sales tax on investments in manufacturing buildings and
machinery. Laws of 1985, ch. 232. With regard to the sales tax
deferral, RCW 82. 60. 030, Laws of 1985, ch. 232, § 3, states: " Appli-
cation for deferral of taxes under this chapter must be made [ to the
Department] before initiation of the construction of the investment
project or acquisition of equipment or machinery."
FINAL DECISION - Page 9 Dockets Nos. 00- 005 to 00- 009

1 In 1986, the Legislature also permitted such manufacturers to
2 take a credit against their B&O tax for each new employee hired at the
3 manufacturing facility. Laws of 1986, ch. 116. With regard to the
4 B&O tax credit, RCW 82. 62. 020, Laws of 1986, ch. 116, § 16, states:
5 Application for tax credits under this chapter must be made before
6 the actual hiring of qualified employment positions."
7
8 Requiring taxpayers to apply for these tax benefits is no idle
9 exercise. In the case of the sales tax deferral program, it serves
10 several purposes. First, it facilitates enforcement of the sales tax
11 and the tax deferral program. The revenue -raising success of the
12 sales tax depends upon it being enforced in the first instance by
13 sellers at the time of sale. The Department re -enforces the tax, so
14 to speak, by auditing sellers, not buyers. Sellers and buyers know
15 this. The application requirement allows the Department to issue a
16 tax exemption certificate which the qualified applicant must then
17 present to its seller at the time of sale. The seller then ( 1) knows
18 with certainty that the buyer is entitled to purchase free of sales
19 tax, and ( 2) has a hassle -free audit trail to support its ( the
20 seller' s) justification for not collecting the sales tax on what would
21 otherwise be a taxable sale. Maintaining the good will of sellers by
22 promoting ease of compliance is essential to the success of the sales
23 tax system. It is not an understatement to say that the sales tax
24 deferral program, with eligibility dependent upon ever- changing
25 county -by -county unemployment statistics, would be bedlam without the
26
27 FINAL DECISION - Page 10 Dockets Nos. 00- 005 to 00- 009

1 provision for a sales tax exemption certificate issued by the
2 Department.
3
4 Second, the application requirement is necessary to enable the
5 Department to identify which taxpayers actually purchase tax- free
6 under the deferral program in order to timely certify the investment
7 project as " operationally completed," the triggering event for the
8 start of the repayment schedule on the deferred taxes. RCW 82. 60. 060.
9
10 Third, the application requirement is necessary for fiscal
11 control of the distressed areas tax relief program. In the case of
12 the sales tax deferral, the Legislature desired to know for its budget
13 planning and control purposes the amount of taxes deferred at the time
14 they were deferred. " The department shall keep a running total of all
15 deferrals granted under this chapter during each fiscal biennium."
16 RCW 82. 60. 040( 2). In the case of the B&O tax credit program, the
17 Legislature placed an overall limit on the dollar amount of the credit
18 which be could claimed in any given year. " The department shall keep
19 a running total of all credits granted under this chapter during each
20 fiscal year. The department shall not allow any credits which would
21 cause the tabulation to exceed seven million five hundred thousand
22 dollars in any fiscal year. 11 RCW 82. 62. 030( 2). Without an
23 application approval process, the Department would have no way to
24 fulfill its legislatively mandated duties in this area.
25

27 FINAL DECISION - Page 11 Dockets Nos. 00- 005 to 00- 009

The Department argues that the requirement for submitting an
application before making an investment or hiring employees is manda-
tory. We agree. One of the requirements of both RCW. 82. 60. 030 and
82. 62. 020, above, is that the person seeking the deferral or credit
must file an application before construction, buying equipment and
machinery, or actual hiring of new employees. Both statutes state
that applications " must be made" before construction, purchase, or
hiring.
The word " must" has legal consequences, and has the same effect
as the word " shall." a Black' s Law Dictionary at 1019 ( 6`h ed. 1990) .
It is well settled that the word " shall" in a statute is presumptively
imperative and operates to create a duty. Crown Cascade, Inc. v.
O' Neal, 100 Wn. 2d 256, 261, 668 P. 2d 585 ( 1983). The word " shall" in
a statute thus imposes a mandatory requirement unless a contrary
legislative intent is apparent. State v. Bryan, 93 Wn. 2d 177, 183,
606 P. 2d 1228 ( 1980). Accord, State v. Q. D., 102 Wn. 2d 19, 685 P. 2d
557 ( 1984). Here, there is simply no evidence—linguistically or
contextually—of a contrary intent.
3 The word " must" perhaps conveys even stronger connotations of imper-
ativeness than the word " shall," at least to Washington lawyers. See
Washington Rules of Appellate Procedure ( RAP) 1. 2.( b) " Words of
Command . . . Unless the context of the rule indicates otherwise:
The word ` must' is used in place of ` should' . . . to emphasize
failure to perform the act in a timely way may result in more severe
than usual sanctions . . . . The word ` shall' is used when referring
to an act that is to be done by an entity other than the appellate
court, a party, or counsel for a party."

2 duty on the Taxpayers to file applications for tax deferral and

9 II
10
11 The Taxpayers claim that ( 1) the Department represented to them
12 that they could not qualify for tax deferrals and credits, ( 2) they
13 reasonably relied upon the Department' s representations and therefore
14 did not attempt to qualify by filing an application, and ( 3) they have
15 been harmed because they have been denied a benefit. The Taxpayers
16 contend that under these circumstances the Department should be
17 equitably estopped from rejecting their applications as untimely.
18
19 The elements of equitable estoppel are: ( 1) an admission state-
20 ment or act inconsistent with the claim afterwards asserted, ( 2)
21 action by the other party on the faith of such admission, statement,
22 or act, and ( 3) injury to such other party resulting from allowing the
23 first party to contradict or repudiate such admission, statement, or
24 act. Harbor Air Service, Inc. v. Board of Tax Appeals, 88 Wn. 2d 359,
25 560 P. 2d 1145 ( 1977). Equitable estoppel runs against the State,
26
27 FINAL DECISION - Page 13 Dockets Nos. 00- 005 to 00- 009

even when acting in its tax collecting capacity. Id. But it is not
lightly invoked. Group Health Cooperative of Puget Sound, Inc. v.
Department of Revenue, 106 Wn. 2d 391, 722 P. 2d 787 ( 1986). Thus, in
addition to the above three elements, a person asserting estoppel
against the government must also show ( 4) it must be necessary to
prevent a manifest injustice and ( 5) the exercise of vital govern-
ment functions would not be impaired. Department of Ecology v.
Theodoratus, 135 Wn. 2d 582, 957 P. 2d 1241 ( 1998).
The Department' s main defense stems from the fact that the record
does not establish that it made any statement to the Taxpayers
concerning its view of their eligibility for distressed areas tax
deferral and credits. The statements made by the Department were made
either to other taxpayers or independent professional accountants in
the course of seminars. In the Department' s view, estoppel may rbe
invoked only by a taxpayer to which the Department has rendered
specific, written advice, and then only as a matter of legislative
direction pursuant to the Taxpayer' s Rights and Responsibilities Act,
RCW Chapter 82. 32A. 4
4 RCW 82. 32A. 020 provides: " The taxpayers of the state of Washington
have: . . . ( 2) The right to rely on specific, official written advice
and written tax reporting instructions from the department of revenue
to that taxpayer, and to have interest, penalties, and in some
instances, tax deficiency assessments waived where the taxpayer has so
relied to their proven detriment . . . ."

Apple Packers Quincy, Inc. v. Department of Revenue, supra, the Court

21 defining manufacturing indicates that these activities should be

Inland Finance Co. v. Inland Motor Car Co., 125 Wash. 301 ( 1913);
24 Lobdell v. Sugar ' N Spice, Inc., 33 Wn. App. 881, 658 P. 2d 1267
1983). See also Franklin County Sheriff' s Office v. Sellers, 97

construed as manufacturing." Valley Fruit, supra at 419. Whether or
not a statute applies to a given set of facts is a question of law.
In sum, even if the Department made its oral statements about the
availability of the distressed areas tax benefits directly to the
Taxpayer, estoppel does not lie against the Department because the
statements were opinions on a question of law.
III
The Taxpayers argue that they should be entitled to refunds on
the related equitable ground of " unjust enrichment." We disagree.
First, the State Supreme Court considered " unfairness" and " manifest
injustice" when it established the rule that the government cannot be
estopped with respect to its representations of law. Department of
Ecology v. Theodoratus, supra.
Second, to the extent that the claim is considered apart from
equitable estoppel, we must reject it because the Taxpayers had an
adequate statutory legal remedy: this very administrative proceeding
or a statutory tax refund action in Thurston County Superior Court
pursuant to RCW 82. 32. 180. Equitable remedies are not available
unless the remedies at law are inadequate. Landry v. Luscher, 95 Wn.
App. 779, 976 P. 2d 1274 ( 1999). The Taxpayers have not alleged any
facts showing the unavailability or inadequacy of the existing
FINAL DECISION - Page 16 Dockets Nos. 00- 005 to 00- 009

1 statutory remedies other than those facts supporting their claim of
2 equitable estoppel.

5
6 The Taxpayers argue that they should be excused from the pre-
7 filing requirement because it would have been a useless act.
8 According to the Taxpayers: " The Washington State Judiciary will not
9 require vain and useless acts. See Orion Corp. v. State, 103 Wn. 2d
10 441, 693 P. 2d 1369 ( 1985)." Chiawana' s Memorandum in Support of

22 The Taxpayers' argument on this point is grounded in the doctrine
23 of exhaustion of administrative remedies, which holds that before a
24 court will entertain claim against the government, a claimant must
25 first exhaust its statutory remedies, if any, within the Executive

1 Branch. Wright v. Woodard, 83 Wn. 2d 378, 518 P. 2d 718 ( 1974); 2
2 Am. Jur. 2d Administrative Law § 505 ( 1994). The doctrine is appli-
cable not only to tax claims ( Wright v. Woodard, supra), but tort

5 1978]), regulatory taking ( i.e., inverse condemnation) claims ( Orion

8
9 The Taxpayers may or may not be correct that they are excused
10 from complying with mandatory statutory procedural requirements on

12 tion because the doctrine of exhaustion of administrative remedies
13 is applicable only to the issue of whether the Judicial Branch can
14 or will exercise its jurisdiction to entertain a claim against the

16 ity, is firmly ensconced in the Executive Branch. We may not increase
17 our statutorily authorized jurisdiction by application of a doctrine

21
22 The Taxpayers argue that the Department cannot apply HB 2295
23 retroactively to them because to do so would impair their " vested
24 rights." The " vested rights doctrine" has long been a cornerstone of
25

1 Washington law. In Gillis v. King County, 42 Wn. 2d 373, 376, 255
2 P. 2d 546 ( 1953), the Court stated:

less of the intention of the legislature, where the effect

may not operate retroactively where the result would be

7
8 The Taxpayers contend that they have a " vested right" to have
9 their claims for tax deferrals and credits considered under the law as

11 Appellants have a vested right to proceed with their
claims for the refunds under the law as it existed at the

activities upon which. their refund claims are based, and

Appellants of that vested right.
14

16
17 The initial inquiry should thus focus on the " law as it existed"
18 at the time the Taxpayers undertook the activities upon which their
19 refund claims are based. The Taxpayers understandably view the Valley
20 Fruit Court' s interpretation of the term " manufacturing" to be part of
21 the law as it existed from its enactment in 1985 until the passage of
22 HB 2295. See Johnson v. Morris, 87 Wn. 2d 922, 557 P. 2d 1299 ( 1976).
23 However, HB 2295 unmistakably indicates that the Legislature intended
24 its subsequent interpretation of the term " manufacturing" to be part
25 of the law as it existed during that same period. " This act is
26
27 FINAL DECISION - Page 19 Dockets Nos. 00 -005 -to 00- 009

1 intended to clarify that this is the intent of the legislature both
2 retroactively and prospectively." ( Emphasis supplied.) Resolution of
3 this issue is analytically important because if HB 2295 is considered
4 to be a mere clarification of legislative intent as to the meaning of
5 an existing law, rather than a substantive change, there canbe no
6 impairment of vested rights. W] hen the legislature acts to
7 construe an ambiguity in a pre- existing statute, it is not legislating
8 retroactively." Carpenter v. Butler, 32 Wn. 2d 371, 379, 201 P. 2d 704
9 1949).
10

12 under the " vested rights" doctrine, we decline to resolve the issue of

16 of government;' and it is not necessary to resolve the matter in order
17 to decide the controversy between the parties. Even if the Valley
18 Fruit interpretation is considered to be the law as it existed at the

1 time the Taxpayers made their investments, the Taxpayers' claim still

4 Because the Taxpayers' remaining arguments on the " vested rights"
5 issue raise only the issue of the substantive provisions of HB 2295 as

8 is whether retroactive application of HB 2295 would deprive the
9 Taxpayers of a vested property right. The Taxpayers cite Olesen v.

11 A vested right, entitled to protection from legislation,
must be something more than a mere expectation based upon
12 an anticipated continuance of existing law; it must have
become a title, legal or equitable, to the present or future
13 enjoyment of property, a demand, or a legal exemption from a
demand by another.

17 deferrals or credits; rather they simply have a mere expectation that
18 if they satisfy the statutory requirements, they would be eligible for

23 of the law. The Valley Packing interpretation related back to the
24 original enactment date of the distressed areas tax deferral and
25 credit statutes, and was therefore part of the existing law at the
